title: Hydrogen and fuel cells

concepts.label: fuel cell
concepts.definition: A galvanic cell whose reactants (here hydrogen and oxygen) are fed in from outside, so its electrodes are not consumed and it runs for as long as it is supplied.

concepts.label: hydrogen oxidation reaction
concepts.definition: The anode (−) half-reaction of a hydrogen fuel cell, H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ in acid (H goes 0 → +1); in base 2H₂ + 4OH⁻ → 4H₂O + 4e⁻.

concepts.label: oxygen reduction reaction
concepts.definition: The cathode (+) half-reaction, O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O in acid (O goes 0 → −2); in base O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻; four electrons per O₂ and the slow step of the cell.

concepts.label: ideal voltage 1.23 V
concepts.definition: E°cell of 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, 1.23 − 0.00 V: the most a hydrogen–oxygen cell can give at 25 °C, equal to the minimum voltage of water electrolysis, and worth 237 kJ per mole of H₂ (ΔG° = −nFE°).

concepts.label: catalyst
concepts.definition: A substance (here a platinum surface) that lowers the energy barrier of a reaction and so speeds it up, without being consumed and without changing the energy released or the cell voltage.

concepts.label: three-phase boundary
concepts.definition: The place where gas pore, electrolyte (ion path) and electron conductor all touch a catalyst grain; the electrode reaction can only run there.

concepts.label: proton-exchange membrane (PEM) cell
concepts.definition: A fuel cell whose electrolyte is a thin solid membrane that conducts only H⁺ from anode to cathode; platinum catalyst, about 60–80 °C, water forms at the cathode.

concepts.label: alkaline and solid-oxide fuel cells
concepts.definition: Fuel cells in which a negative ion crosses from cathode to anode and water forms at the anode: OH⁻ through KOH solution (alkaline, Apollo) or O²⁻ through a hot ceramic at 600–1000 °C (solid oxide, no platinum needed).

concepts.label: overpotential
concepts.definition: The voltage lost inside a working cell, compared with its ideal voltage, to drive slow electrode reactions, push ions through the electrolyte and overcome gas starvation; it leaves as heat.

concepts.label: polarisation curve
concepts.definition: The plot of cell voltage against current density (A/cm²): about 1.0 V at zero current, a gently falling working region near 0.7 V, then a collapse when the gas supply cannot keep up.

concepts.label: efficiency = V / 1.48 V
concepts.definition: The fraction of hydrogen's heat of combustion (286 kJ/mol, liquid water) delivered as electricity equals the cell voltage divided by 1.48 V: 83% for the ideal 1.23 V, about 47% at 0.70 V.

concepts.label: heat-engine (Carnot) limit
concepts.definition: The ceiling 1 − T_cold/T_hot (temperatures in kelvin) on any machine that turns heat into work; a fuel cell converts chemical energy to electricity directly, so the limit does not apply to it.

concepts.label: fuel-cell stack
concepts.definition: Many cells pressed together in a row so that their voltages add while the same current, set by the plate area, flows through all of them; power = cells × volts per cell × current.

concepts.label: energy per kg vs per litre
concepts.definition: Hydrogen holds about 39 kWh of heat per kilogram, three times petrol, but as a gas very little per litre (about 0.08 g/L at 1 bar, 39 g/L at 700 bar, 71 g/L as a liquid at −253 °C).

concepts.label: round-trip efficiency
concepts.definition: Energy returned by electrolyser + fuel cell divided by the energy put in; since the charge is the same both ways it equals fuel-cell voltage ÷ electrolyser voltage, roughly a third in practice.

namedOnly: current density (A/cm², introduced as the unit of the polarisation curve's x-axis)
activation, ohmic and mass-transport losses (described as 'slow reactions', 'ion traffic', 'gas starvation'; internal resistance is taught in Real batteries)
heat of combustion / enthalpy (used as 'the 286 kJ you get as heat by burning one mole of H₂')
liquid-water (higher) vs steam (lower) heating value, 1.48 V vs 1.25 V (one note)
bipolar plate (described by function, not named)
yttria-stabilised zirconia (given as ZrO₂ with some Y₂O₃)
hydrogen crossover (the 'trace of hydrogen leaking through the membrane' behind the 1.0 V open-circuit reading)
flooding of electrode pores by product water
petrol and Li-ion energy densities (approximate comparison figures)
hydrogen–bromine and other H₂-anode cells (cathode toggle in step 3)
summary: Running example: a hydrogen–oxygen cell fed from a tank holding 0.20 g (0.100 mol) of H₂, which carries the same 5.36 Ah as the 6.54 g zinc strip of the Daniell cell; it is followed from 'fed, not used up' through its half-reactions (water electrolysis reversed), the 1.23 V rung on the potential ladder (the hydrogen anode is the SHE), catalyst and three-phase boundary, the PEM / alkaline / solid-oxide variants (which ion crosses, where water forms), the polarisation curve (0.70 V at 1 A/cm²), efficiency = V / 1.48 V, stacking, storage per kg vs per litre and the electrolyser + fuel cell round trip (V_out / V_in). Capstone: a polarisation-curve and stack simulator (catalyst, membrane, air vs oxygen, current density, number of cells, plate area) that must reach 1 kW or 100 kW and reports efficiency, hydrogen use and heat. Hooks for later lessons: 'a catalyst changes speed, not volts', the three voltage losses and the V–i curve (Real batteries), power peak vs efficiency, voltages add in a row (series), and oxygen from the air as a cathode reactant (zinc–air, corrosion).
